sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Pele** ​(*pele*) — ‌Volcanoes, ‌Fire, Lightning, ​Dance ​· ​One who ​shapes ​the sacred ‌land ​(Hawaiian) — ​belongs ‌to ​the Polynesian ‌tradition, ​where it ‌is ​catalogued under ​the ​domain ​"Volcanoes, Fire, ​Lightning, ‌Dance". The ​name ‌means "One ​who ‌shapes ​the sacred ‌land ​(Hawaiian)".

**Pele** ‌is ​volcanoes, fire, ​lightning, ‌dance. ‌The name ‌means ​"One who ​shapes ‌the sacred ​land ​(Hawaiian)" ‌and belongs ​to ​the polynesian ‌tradition.

​PuniCodex restores ‌the ​name as ​**Pele** ​and ​serves its ‌temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/pele/). ‌The restoration ​needs ​no ‌distinctive letters ‌or ‌diacritics its ‌ASCII ​form would ‌lose, ​which ​places the ​name ‌in Tier ​2. ​The plain ​ASCII ‌form ​*pele* survives ​as ​a modern ‌convenience ​imposed by ‌the ​early ‌domain-name system; ​the ‌restoration, not ‌the ​fallback, is ​the ​form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​modern ​Polynesian orthographies; ​macron ​usage ​follows each ‌tradition’s ​reference ​dictionaries. Etymologically ‌the ​name ‌means ​"One who ‌shapes ​the ​sacred land ​(Hawaiian)".

​The ​ASCII form ‌*pele* ​survives ‌only because ​the ‌early ​domain-name ‌system could ​not ‌carry ​diacritics; it ​is ‌a ‌technological compromise, ‌not ​an ​ancient spelling. ‌The ​Unicode ​restoration ‌**Pele** recovers ​the ​full ‌diacritic detail ​of ‌the ​scholarly transliteration ​directly ​in ​the ‌address bar. ‌The ​restoration ‌needs no ​distinctive ​letters ‌or diacritics ‌its ‌ASCII ‌form would ​lose, ‌which ​places ​the name ​in ‌Tier ​2.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ​**p** ​→ ​**P** — ‌Same
​- ‌**e** ​→ **e** ‌— ​Same
‌- **l** ‌→ ​**l** ​— Same
​- ​**e** ‌→ **e** ‌— ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/pele/** — ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

‌- ​**pele** ‌— ​The canonical ‌restored ​form ​Pele.

​For the ​modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest approximation ‌is: ​Say ‌"pele" ​with the ‌stress ​and ‌length ​implied by ​the ‌scholarly ‌restoration ‌"Pele".

​The ASCII ​form ‌"pele" ​is ​a DNS ‌compromise; ​the ​restoration ‌"Pele" preserves ​the ‌name's ​scholarly ​dignity.

The ​pronunciation ​given ‌above ‌reconstructs the ​sound ‌world ​in ​which ‌Pele was ‌invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should not ‌expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not ​a performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌restoration ​Pele ‌keeps the ​prosodic ‌information ‌visible ​even when ​the ​name ​is ‌typed in ‌plain ​ASCII.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Pele ‌place volcanoes, ​fire, ​lightning, dance ​at ​the ​center of ‌a ​living mythological ​world.

‌### Origins ​(Myth)

‌Pele appears ​in ‌polynesian tradition ​as ​volcanoes, fire, ​lightning, ​dance. The ​name's ‌meaning, ​"One who ‌shapes ​the sacred ‌land ​(Hawaiian)", shapes ‌the ​narratives told ‌about ​this figure.

​### ‌Worship and ‌Memory ‌(Cult)

Devotees ​and ​later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ​Pele ​in ritual, ‌text, ​and iconography, ​ensuring ‌the name ​survived ‌into the ​modern ​scholarly record.

​The ​myths of ‌Pele ‌survive ​in fragments, ‌summaries, ​and later ​retellings. ‌Each version ‌reflects ‌the interests ‌of ​its tellers ‌— ​poets, priests, ​philosophers, ​and scholars. ‌The ​PuniCodex ​entry does ​not ‌privilege a ​single ​version; it ​gathers ‌the attestations ​so ‌that readers ​can ‌compare them. ​The ‌restoration Pele ‌gives ​the ​figure a ​stable ​name around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Pele ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Polynesian ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Pele, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​volcanoes ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
To ​contemplate Pele ‌is ‌to ​hold the ​idea ​of ​volcanoes, Fire, ​Lightning, ‌Dance ​in the ​mind ‌and ​to ask ‌what ​of ‌it endures. ​The ​name means ​"One ​who ​shapes the ‌sacred ​land ‌(Hawaiian)" — ​and ‌a ​name that ‌carries ​its ‌meaning so ​openly ​invites ‌meditation rather ‌than ‌mere recollection. ​The ​tradition ‌remembers the ​name ​as ‌volcanoes, Fire, ​Lightning, ​Dance ‌· One ​who ‌shapes ​the sacred ​land ​(Hawaiian).

​Sit with ‌the ‌restored ​form — ‌Pele ​— and ​the ‌diacritics ‌themselves become ‌the ‌practice: ​each mark ‌is ​a ​small act ​of ‌attention, ​a refusal ​to ​let ‌the plain ​ASCII ​form *pele* ​stand ‌in ​for the ‌whole. ​What ‌the tradition ​preserved ‌in ‌this name, ​the ​restoration ​asks the ​reader ‌to ‌preserve in ​turn.
